Prompts

Articulate what went wrong in the father’s reasoning.

  3. 3 Provide 5 cases from history in which this type of circular argument is used.

1

Composite Response

Prompt 1: A father tell his son that all caves are man-made and justifies this by referring to the fact that all caves he has thus far examined have been man-made. The boy finds a cave that does not look man-made, but the father tells him that inductive inference allow him to conclude that this cave is also man-made, and adds this cave as another data point in his collection of data points on the side of all caves being man-made. Articulate what went wrong in the father’s reasoning.

The case matters because it shows how a belief can train itself not to lose.

The father's reasoning is a useful case study because it does not look absurd at first glance. It begins with repeated experience and the confidence that repeated experience often deserves. The problem appears when that confidence hardens into a rule that is no longer willing to let contrary evidence count.

That is what makes the loop epistemically dangerous. A belief initially formed by something like induction turns into a self-protective machine. The original evidence is treated not as support that could be revised, but as a license to reinterpret every future anomaly back into line.

The page should therefore help the reader see how closed loops emerge gradually. Bad reasoning often starts with a reasonable pattern and becomes distorted when the pattern is made invulnerable.

Misapplication of Inductive Reasoning Inductive reasoning involves making generalized conclusions from specific instances. It relies on the assumption that if a certain number of cases of a phenomenon have a particular characteristic, then future cases will likely have the same characteristic. The father concludes that all caves are man-made because every cave he has previously encountered was man-made. However, inductive reasoning is not absolute and requires open-mindedness to new evidence that could contradict earlier conclusions. The discovery of a natural cave by the son should serve as a counterexample that challenges the father’s generalization, rather than being dismissed.

Confirmation Bias Confirmation bias is a tendency to search for, interpret, favor, and recall information in a way that confirms one’s preconceived beliefs or hypotheses, while giving disproportionately less consideration to alternative possibilities. The father’s decision to label the newly found cave as man-made without investigation exemplifies confirmation bias. Instead of reevaluating his hypothesis in light of new evidence (the son’s cave), he prematurely includes it as another supporting instance, thereby ignoring signs that might indicate its natural origin.

Ignoring Counterexamples A single counterexample is sufficient to invalidate a universal generalization made through inductive reasoning. The son’s finding of a cave that does not appear man-made challenges the father’s claim that all caves are man-made. Proper scientific and logical methodology would require the father to investigate this new cave and, if found to be natural, to revise or reject his original hypothesis.

Hasty Generalization The father may also be guilty of hasty generalization—drawing a conclusion based on a sample size that is too small or unrepresentative. Just because all caves known to him are man-made does not logically entail that all caves everywhere are so. The diversity and vastness of geological formations should caution against such broad conclusions from a limited dataset.

Circular Reasoning The father’s argument is somewhat circular: he is using the assumption (all caves are man-made) to interpret new findings (the cave found by his son), and then using those findings to support the original assumption. This circularity prevents any possibility of falsifying his hypothesis, which is a key aspect of scientific inquiry.

Hasty generalization The father has generalized that all caves are man-made based on a limited set of observations (the caves he has examined so far). This hasty generalization is unjustified, as it is impossible to examine every single cave in existence and conclude that they are all man-made.

Confirmation bias The father seems to be exhibiting confirmation bias, which is the tendency to selectively seek out and interpret information in a way that confirms one’s preexisting beliefs or hypotheses. When the son finds a cave that does not look man-made, the father dismisses this contradictory evidence and continues to hold onto his belief that all caves are man-made.

Failure to consider alternative explanations The father fails to consider alternative explanations for the existence of caves, such as natural geological processes like erosion, tectonic activity, or the action of water and ice over long periods of time.

Misunderstanding of inductive inference The father misunderstands the nature of inductive inference. While induction can be used to make probable generalizations, it does not lead to certainties or conclusive proofs. Each new observation or data point should be evaluated objectively, and generalizations should be updated or revised if contradictory evidence is found.

  1. Reasonable starting point: Repeated cases can justify provisional confidence.
  2. Corruption point: Confidence becomes dogmatism when future counterevidence is no longer allowed real authority.
  3. Loop formation: The belief starts managing anomalies instead of learning from them.
  4. Pedagogical value: The case shows how epistemic vice can grow out of initially ordinary inference.

What to notice

  • Leave the reader with a sharper question about Insatiable Loops, not just a cleaner paraphrase.
  • Track the movement in the exchange: A father tell his son that all caves are man-made and justifies this, Acknowledge the limitations of inductive reasoning and avoid making, and Remain open to contradictory evidence and be willing to revise his should show where the reasoning gains support and where it still strains.
  • Watch how the section calibrates confidence rather than merely defending a conclusion.
2

Composite Response

Prompt 2: How might the son respond to his father to make salient the logical circularity in his argument.

The son's best reply is to show that the father's rule protects itself by redefining the evidence.

The circularity becomes clear once the son notices that the father's conclusion is being used to police the interpretation of every new case. A cave that does not look man-made is not allowed to count as evidence against the theory because the theory itself is invoked to insist that it must somehow still be man-made. The conclusion is doing double duty as both result and filter.

That is what makes the loop 'insatiable.' It can swallow any apparent counterexample by reinterpretation. The father is no longer learning from the evidence; he is teaching the evidence what it is allowed to mean.

A strong response from the son should therefore emphasize not just disagreement, but method. He should point out that a claim which cannot, even in principle, be endangered by a contrary-looking case is no longer being tested honestly.

Son “Dad, when you say that all caves including this new one are man-made because all the caves you’ve seen so far were man-made, aren’t you assuming what you’re supposed to prove?”

Son “Well, it seems like you’re using your assumption that all caves are man-made to conclude that this new cave must be man-made, too. But isn’t that the question we’re trying to answer? Whether all caves are actually man-made?”

Son “But consider this: what if I told you all birds I’ve seen are black, and then I concluded that a newly discovered white bird must also be black because all birds I’ve seen before were black? That wouldn’t make sense, right? I’d be ignoring new evidence just to fit my previous assumption.”

Son “Is it? If we use the previous information about caves to automatically classify any new cave as man-made, we are not allowing for the possibility that there could be natural caves. We’re just going in circles – assuming all caves are man-made because we classify them as such, without testing if they actually are. It’s a bit like saying what I want to prove is true because I say it is.”

Premise 1 All the caves you’ve examined so far are man-made. Premise 2: You assume that all caves are man-made (the conclusion you want to reach). Conclusion: Therefore, this new cave that doesn’t look man-made must also be man-made.

  1. Conclusion as filter: The father's belief decides in advance how every new cave must be interpreted.
  2. Counterexample absorption: Apparent disconfirming cases are neutralized rather than allowed genuine evidential force.
  3. Methodological criticism: The real problem is not only the conclusion but the self-protective way it handles evidence.

What to notice

  • Leave the reader with a sharper question about circularity, not just a cleaner paraphrase.
  • Track the movement in the exchange: Circularity and A father tell his son that all caves are man-made and justifies this should show where the reasoning gains support and where it still strains.
  • Watch how the section calibrates confidence rather than merely defending a conclusion.
3

Composite Response

Prompt 3: Provide 5 cases from history in which this type of circular argument is used.

Historical cases matter because circularity often survives by appearing explanatory.

Historical examples are useful here because circular arguments are rarely announced in neon. They often sound like explanations: the doctrine is true because the tradition says so, the tradition is trustworthy because it teaches the doctrine, the leader is right because the movement succeeds, and the movement succeeds because the leader is right.

That is why readers need real cases. Circularity is easier to spot when one sees how institutions, ideologies, and public narratives can stabilize themselves by making the conclusion double as its own credential.

The page should therefore use history to train detection. The goal is not only to condemn old mistakes but to recognize the same structure when it reappears in modern form.

Geocentric Model of the Universe In medieval Europe, the prevailing view was that the Earth was the center of the universe (the geocentric model), primarily supported by religious and philosophical beliefs. Defenders of this model often used circular reasoning by citing religious texts that assumed Earth’s central position as proof of that same central position. They would argue that Earth is the center of the universe because texts, interpreted to say so, must be correct because they come from an infallible source, thus reasserting the original assumption without independent proof.

Racial Science in the 19th and Early 20th Century Proponents of racial science, particularly during the period of colonization and the early 20th century eugenics movement, often used circular arguments to justify racial hierarchies. They would begin with the assumption that certain races were inherently inferior and then interpret social and economic disparities as evidence of this inferiority, rather than considering external factors like discrimination or unequal opportunities.

Witch Hunts in the Early Modern Period During the witch hunts in Europe and colonial America (approximately 1450 to 1750), accusations of witchcraft were often justified using circular reasoning. The existence of witches was ‘proven’ by confessions obtained under torture or duress; those confessions served as evidence that the torture was justified because it confirmed the witches’ existence. This logic was famously critiqued during the Salem witch trials.

Divine Right of Kings The doctrine of the Divine Right of Kings was used to justify monarchial authority by asserting that kings are appointed by God and thus rightfully hold absolute power. The circularity comes from the use of Biblical authority or religious doctrine to prove the king’s divine appointment, which in turn was used to justify the religious authority’s legitimacy. Essentially, the king is king because God made it so, and we know God made it so because the king (and his supporting clerics) tells us so, using the same religious texts that establish and support their power.

McCarthyism and the Red Scare In the 1950s, during the Red Scare in the United States, Senator Joseph McCarthy and others argued that the presence of communists in government and other institutions was widespread and that any denial of being a communist was seen as evidence of deceit typical of communists. The circular logic here was that if you denied being a communist, your denial was just what a communist would do, thus ‘confirming’ your communist affiliation. This circular reasoning led to widespread fear and persecution without substantive evidence.

Geocentric model of the universe For centuries, the geocentric model of the universe, which placed the Earth at the center of the cosmos, was widely accepted. One of the arguments used to support this model was that if the Earth were moving, objects should fall off its surface. However, this argument assumed the very thing it was trying to prove: that the Earth was stationary.

Divine command theory In religious philosophy, the divine command theory asserts that moral truths are true because they are commanded by God. However, this reasoning is circular because it assumes that God is good and worthy of obedience, which is itself a moral claim that requires justification.

Argument from design (watchmaker analogy) The watchmaker analogy, used by philosophers like William Paley, argues that the complexity of the universe implies the existence of an intelligent designer (God). However, this argument assumes the conclusion it is trying to prove – the existence of God – as a premise for the analogy.

Aristotelian physics In his physics, Aristotle argued that objects fell because of their natural tendency to seek their “natural place.” Heavy objects fell because their natural place was the center of the universe (Earth), while light objects rose because their natural place was the celestial spheres. This reasoning was circular because it assumed the very thing it was trying to explain: the motion of objects.

Phrenology Phrenology, a pseudoscience popular in the 19th century, claimed that personality traits and mental abilities could be determined by the shape of the skull. Phrenologists would feel bumps on the skull and attribute them to certain traits, but their interpretation of these bumps was based on the very assumptions they were trying to prove.

  1. Conclusion as credential: The claim is treated as evidence for itself through a surrounding authority structure.
  2. Institutional reinforcement: Groups can normalize circularity by embedding it in education, ritual, or identity.
  3. Explanatory disguise: The loop often sounds informative because it moves through several words before returning to itself.
  4. Modern relevance: Historical examples matter because the same structure keeps reappearing under new banners.

What to notice

  • Track the movement in the exchange: A father tell his son that all caves are man-made and justifies this should show where the reasoning gains support and where it still strains.

Dialectical Turn

The exchange around Insatiable Loops includes a real movement of judgment.

One pedagogical value of this page is that the prompts do not merely ask for more content. They sometimes force a model to retreat, concede, revise a category, or reframe the answer after the curator's pressure exposes a weakness.

That movement should be read as part of the argument. The important lesson is not simply that an AI changed its wording, but that a better prompt can make a prior stance answerable to logic, counterexample, or conceptual pressure.

  1. The prompt sequence includes reconsideration: the response is revised after the weakness in the first framing becomes visible.

What to notice

  • Track the turn in Insatiable Loops: identify what the first answer missed and what pressure forced the later answer to change.
  • Do not treat concession as decoration; on this page, the revision is part of the argument about Insatiable Loops.
  • Ask whether the later stance is genuinely stronger, or merely more cautious in tone.

Synthesis

What ties this page together.

The best route is to track how evidence changes credence, how justification differs from psychological comfort, and how skepticism can discipline thought without paralyzing it.

The recurring pressure is false certainty: treating a feeling of obviousness, a social consensus, or a useful assumption as if it had already earned the status of knowledge.

Start with A father tell his son that all caves are man-made and justifies this. Without that first grip, Insatiable Loops can sound weighty while staying hard to use.

Read this page as part of the wider Epistemology branch: the prompts point inward to the topic, but they also point outward to neighboring questions that keep the topic honest.

For a companion resource on calibration, credence, and structured rational judgment, see Credencing.com.
